speeches.speaker: Nigel Scullion
speeches.brief: The Senate Standing Committee on Community Affairs presented its report on the Child Support Legislation Amendment (Reform of the Child Support Scheme—New Formula and Other Measures) Bill 2006, and ordered the report to be printed.

speeches.speaker: Santo Santoro
speeches.brief: The bill introduces a new child support formula based on Australian research on the costs of children, with changes including an "income shares" approach, recognition of care for 14% or more of the time, and equal treatment of first and second families. From 1 January 2007, the Social Security Appeals Tribunal will gain expanded powers to review child support decisions, and from 1 July 2008, the new formula will be implemented alongside aligned income definitions for child support and family tax benefit.

speeches.speaker: Chris Evans
speeches.brief: Labor supported the Child Support Legislation Amendment Bill 2006, which introduces a new child support formula based on actual costs of raising children, but expressed serious concern about the lack of protection for low-income families who may face income reductions, noting that 55–60% of single-parent households could receive lower payments under the new formula. The Greens also supported the bill subject to amendments, warning that the combined impact of welfare changes may cause further financial hardship for vulnerable families.

Senator Chris Evans moved an amendment expressing serious concern that the government's child support bill fails to protect low-income families, mismanages transitional arrangements, does not quantify the financial impact on existing customers, lacks up‑to‑date demographic data, imposed an unreasonably short committee inquiry, and introduces overly complex changes.

speeches.speaker: Rachel Siewert
speeches.brief: The Greens argued that the new child support formula fails to adequately recognise unpaid care costs, disproportionately harming low-income families and single mothers, and noted that only half of non-resident parents meet their obligations. The party supported the bill with amendments to address shared care arrangements and compliance issues.

speeches.speaker: Glenn Sterle
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Child Support Legislation Amendment Bill 2006 improves fairness for second families and children, but criticised the rushed consultation process and inadequate time given to the committee and witnesses, despite valuable earlier reviews such as the House of Representatives Standing Committee’s *Every picture tells a story* report and the Parkinson review.

Senator Chris Evans moved an amendment to the child support bill, expressing serious concern about the lack of protection for low-income families, poor handling of transitional arrangements, failure to quantify financial impacts on existing customers, missing demographic data, the unreasonably short committee inquiry timeframe, and the overly complex nature of the changes.

speeches.speaker: Rachel Siewert
speeches.brief: The Greens moved amendments requiring a parent's current income, not just a tax assessment, to prove financial hardship for child support, which the government and Labor accepted. A further Greens amendment for an independent review of the combined impact of child support and welfare-to-work changes on low-income families was rejected by the government but supported by Labor.
